---
title: "DST pitfalls"
subtitle: "14 mistakes with Statistics Denmark (DST) registers that give a wrong result without a clear error message"
date: last-modified
pagetitle: "Pitfalls with Statistics Denmark (DST) data"
description: "Common errors with Danish registers at Statistics Denmark (DST): DODSAARS ends in 2001, BEF is a status snapshot, date formats and immortal time bias."
---

Use this page as a checklist before you trust a result, and come back to it when
a number looks too good or too small. It lists 13 mistakes that are easy to make
with DST registers and hard to notice: most of them give no error message, and
the result is just wrong. Each one says what goes wrong, how to check your own
data, and what to do instead. If your code stopped with an error, go to
[Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd) instead.

## 1. Four death registers - `dodsaars` stops in 2001 {#death-registers}

Four registers have similar names, and the one whose name looks like "the death
register" ended in 2001:

  | Register       | DST's name           | Covers             | Use it for                |
  | -------------- | -------------------- | ------------------ | ------------------------- |
  | `dod`          | Døde i Danmark       | 1970-2025, ongoing | Censoring at death        |
  | `dodsaars`     | Dødsårssagsregistret | 1970-2001, closed  | Cause of death, to 2001   |
  | `dodsaasg`     | Dødsårsagsregister   | 2002-2022, closed  | Cause of death, 2002-2022 |
  | `dodsaarsager` | Dødsårsagsregister   | 2022-2024, ongoing | Cause of death, 2022 on   |

Names (in DST's own spelling) and coverage are from [DST's register
overview](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/forskningvariabellister/Oversigt%20over%20registre.html),
read in November 2026.

The date of death is in `dod`, which covers the whole period on its own. The
cause of death is split across the three others, so a study spanning 1995 to
2024 needs all three, and none of them alone will tell you it is incomplete.
`dodsaasg` and `dodsaarsager` both cover 2022, so check that deaths in 2022 are
not counted twice when you stack them.

::: {.callout-warning}
**If you censor on `dodsaars`, everyone who died after 2001 looks alive.** There
is no error and no warning. They stay in your risk set until the end of
follow-up, so your survival curves are too good and your rates are too low. For a
study running past 2001, use `dod`.
:::

```r
library(fastreg) # read_register()
library(dplyr) # semi_join, select, collect

# Date of death for censoring: dod, not dodsaars
death <- read_register("dod") %>%
  rename_with(tolower)

death_person <- death %>%
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort_pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>% # only the cohort's pnr's
  select(pnr, death_date = doddato) %>% # doddato, NOT d_dodsdto
  collect()
```

::: {.callout-note}
**Two things to check on your own project before you rely on this.**

- **Is `dod` in your delivery, and does it reach far enough back?** Your project
  received the years it ordered, not necessarily all of 1970-2025. Check with
  `read_register("dod") %>% summarise(min(doddato), max(doddato)) %>% collect()`.
- **Is it converted to parquet?** On some projects `dod` sits only as a raw SAS (a statistics program)
  file, so `read_register()` will not find it and you read it with
  `haven::read_sas()` instead. Ask your data manager for the path.

Only if `dod` turns out not to cover your early years do you need `dodsaars` as
well, and then you stack the two and rename so the date columns match. Do not do
it by default: both registers cover 1970 to 2001, so stacking them can count
those deaths twice.
:::

## 2. RAM is shared - clean up after large extractions

RAM (the server's working memory) is shared by everyone on the server. One
oversized extraction slows the server for all users, and DST closes processes
automatically when the memory is close to full ([DST's guide on reducing RAM
use](https://www.dst.dk/Site/Dst/SingleFiles/GetArchiveFile.aspx?fi=4500415120635&fo=0&ext=forskning),
PDF in Danish), so it can also cost you your unsaved work.

```r
# Filter early - never collect() first
lmdb <- read_register("lmdb") %>%
  rename_with(tolower) # lazy connection - no RAM used yet (fastreg gets the path)
# Without fastreg: open_dataset("path/to/lmdb/") %>% rename_with(tolower)

result <- lmdb %>%
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort_pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>% # only the cohort's pnr's
  filter(substr(atc, 1, 4) == "N06D") %>% # filter before collect
  select(pnr, atc, eksd) %>%
  collect() # only now is data moved to R

# Free large objects when you are done with them
rm(lmdb) # delete the lazy connection - it does not use much, but it is good practice
gc() # free the memory of removed objects
```

::: {.callout-tip}
To find out *which* object is filling the memory, see [Seeing your memory use
from inside R](good-coding-practice.qmd#see-ram-in-r): `gc()` for the session
total and `object.size()` for the culprit. More habits (save often, partial
loading, Task Manager) are in [Mind your RAM in the shared
environment](good-coding-practice.qmd#mind-your-ram).
:::

## 3. `rename_with(tolower)` must be called on each register {#tolower}

Raw column names vary by register and year: `PNR`, `pnr`, `Pnr`, `V_CPR`. If you
forget it, `semi_join(..., by = "pnr")` stops with "Column `pnr` not found",
even though the column is there under another spelling.

**The rule:** every `open_dataset()` or `read_register()` call ends with
`%>% rename_with(tolower)` as the first step in your pipe. See [Extracting data
step by step](extraction-step-by-step.qmd) for explanation and example.

## 4. Date columns are not always in Date format {#4-date-columns-are-not-always-in-date-format}

Dates arrive in several formats. They look the same when printed but behave
differently.

  | Format      | Example                 | What `class()` returns | What to do                                  |
  | ----------- | ----------------------- | ---------------------- | ------------------------------------------- |
  | Date        | `2020-05-15`            | `"Date"`               | Nothing - can be used directly              |
  | Character   | `"2020-05-15"`          | `"character"`          | `as.Date(column)`                           |
  | Datetime    | `"2020-05-15 14:32:00"` | `"POSIXct" "POSIXt"`   | `as.Date(column)` after `collect()`         |
  | SAS integer | `21990`                 | `"numeric"`            | `as.Date(column, origin = "1960-01-01")`    |

**The rule:** always check `class()` on a date column before using it in
calculations.

```r
class(lpr_a_kontakt$kont_starttidspunkt) # "POSIXct" "POSIXt" - datetime, not Date
# Fix - AFTER collect(), when the data are in R (see the warning below):
mutate(date = as.Date(kont_starttidspunkt))

class(bef$foed_dag) # "Date" - can be used directly
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Filter a datetime column with a datetime, not a date"}
A datetime and a date are two different types, and on a lazy table (before
`collect()`) the engines do not reliably convert between them. What follows was
measured on one DST project server, on `lpr_a_kontakt`, with fastreg 0.14.1,
duckdb 2.0.0, arrow 21.0.0.1 and duckplyr 1.2.2. Other versions may behave
differently, which is the reason to run the count check below on your own
server:

- `filter(as.Date(kont_starttidspunkt) >= as.Date("2023-01-01"))` on a table
  from `fastreg::read_parquet_dataset()` ran without an error but returned 0
  rows, although millions of rows match. Others have seen a `rapi` error from
  the same pattern.
- The same line on a table from `duckplyr::read_parquet_duckdb()` stops with
  `This operation cannot be carried out by DuckDB`.
- Comparing the column with a datetime created before the pipe gave the same,
  correct count on both.

```r
# Wrong on a lazy table - a date where the column is a datetime
filter(as.Date(kont_starttidspunkt) >= as.Date("2023-01-01")) # 0 rows or an error, see the list above
filter(kont_starttidspunkt >= as.Date("2023-01-01")) # kept EVERY row on a read_parquet_duckdb() table (synthetic data, duckplyr 1.2.1, duckdb 1.5.2)

# Right - make the cut-off a datetime first, then compare datetime with datetime
cutoff <- as.POSIXct("2023-01-01", tz = "UTC")
filter(kont_starttidspunkt >= cutoff)
```

Convert to a plain date with `as.Date()` after `collect()`, when the data are
in R. After any date filter, compare `count()` before and after to confirm that
the filter did what you meant: a filter that keeps nothing, or everything, is
the warning sign.

`as.Date()` on a datetime uses UTC (Coordinated Universal Time) unless you give it a `tz`. If the collected
column carries another time zone (check `attr(x, "tzone")`), a contact just
after midnight lands on the previous day; `as.Date(x, tz = "Europe/Copenhagen")`
keeps the local date.
:::

## 5. BEF is a status snapshot - not a live register

BEF (the population register) is a status register: it records the population on a reference date, not
continuously. DST classifies every register as one of four [reference
types](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/generelt-om-data/registre-og-referencetyper):
Status (a snapshot on one date, which is BEF), Statusperiode (population fixed
on a date, values accumulated over a period), Forløb (rows with a start and an
end date) and Hændelse (one row per event, with one date). The type tells you
what a row means. BEF's reference date is the last day of a quarter (31
December for the annual file). Since 2008, BEF is also delivered quarterly
(March, June, September, December).

::: {.callout-note}
**`year == 2020` meaning 1 January 2020 is a project convention.** In many
projects BEF snapshots are renamed so that `year == 2020` refers to the
population composition as of 1 January 2020, but that does not follow from DST's
delivery naming. Confirm the convention in your project guide.

See DST's official BEF documentation: [statistikdokumentation/befolkningen
→](https://www.dst.dk/da/Statistik/dokumentation/statistikdokumentation/befolkningen)
:::

A person is in a BEF file only if they were alive and living in Denmark on that
file's reference date. DST's file `BEF202012` is the status on 31 December 2020,
so a person who died in June 2020 is in `BEF201912` and `BEF202003`, but not in
`BEF202006` or any later file. Which file your project calls `year == 2020`
depends on the convention above, so a filter on `year` cannot tell you who was
alive on a given date.

```r
# WRONG: do not use BEF to check "alive on a specific date"
bef_2020 <- bef %>%
  filter(year == 2020) # everyone alive and resident on that file's reference date
# - including those who die after that date

# CORRECT: combine with dod (not dodsaars - see pitfall 1) to exclude deaths
index_date <- as.Date("2020-06-30") # your index date

deaths <- read_register("dod") %>% # without fastreg: open_dataset("path/to/dod/")
  rename_with(tolower) %>%
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort_pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>%
  select(pnr, doddato) %>%
  collect()

bef_alive <- bef_2020 %>%
  semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort_pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE) %>%
  select(pnr) %>%
  distinct() %>% # one row per person (BEF is quarterly)
  collect() %>%
  left_join(deaths, by = "pnr") %>%
  filter(is.na(doddato) | doddato > index_date) # alive at index date
```

## 6. The "a" in `lpr_a_diagnose` does not mean A-type diagnoses {#lpr-a-not-a-diagnoses}

DST describes the LPR_A tables as an "LPR analyse model" in [its release note
from June
2025](https://www.dst.dk/da/TilSalg/data-til-forskning/nyt-og-meddelelser/2025/nyt-om-grunddata-2-kvartal-2025),
which is the likely origin of the "a" in the table name. It does not mean that
the table holds only A-diagnoses (aktionsdiagnose, the main diagnosis of a
contact).

LPR3 (the patient register from 2019) has two diagnosis types, and the table holds both: A (aktionsdiagnose, main
diagnosis) and B (bidiagnose, secondary diagnosis). G (grundmorbus, underlying
condition) is an LPR2 (the patient register up to 2019) type and is not reported in LPR3. The six LPR2 types and
their years are in [Understand LPR (the National Patient Register)](understand-lpr.qmd#diagtype). So you still
choose the types yourself with a filter on `diag_kode_type`:

```r
lpr_a_diagnose %>%
  filter(diag_kode_type %in% c("A", "B")) %>% # state the types you want; do not assume the table is A only
  ...
```

## 7. Categorical codes are not consistent across registers

The same variable can have different coding in different registers - different
type (numeric vs. character), different values, or both.

The case that costs most is ICD-10. LPR stores it with a Danish `D` in front
(`DE119`), the cause-of-death registers and the cancer register store the plain
WHO (World Health Organization) code (`E119`). A code list built for one matches nothing in the other, and
the habit of stripping the D turns `E119` into `119`. See [ICD (International Classification of Diseases) codes and the
D-prefix](understand-lpr.qmd#d-prefix-not-everywhere).

In practice you extract demographic variables (sex, age) from BEF and rarely
need to compare the same variable in another register. But if you do, always
check with `table()` and `class()` before using the variable:

```r
table(register_a$koen) # what are the actual values and types?
class(register_a$koen)
table(register_b$koen)
class(register_b$koen)
```

## 8. `!!` (bang-bang) forgotten in lazy evaluation {#bang-bang}

When filtering with a local R vector inside a lazy query, dplyr first looks for
a *column* with that name; only if there is none does it copy in the values of
your R object. Usually that works. The trap is a name clash: if your local
object has the same name as a column, the column wins and you get a wrong result
or a confusing message.

```r
# Example: a year list against bef (the principle applies to any local R vector)
year <- c(2018, 2019, 2020) # local R vector - unluckily named like the column

# WRONG - "year" is taken to be the column, so this compares the column with itself
bef %>% filter(year %in% year) # keeps every row, or a confusing error

# CORRECT - !! says: "use the local R vector"
bef %>% filter(year %in% !!year)
```

::: {.callout-note}
This guide puts `!!` in front of every local R object used inside `filter()`,
`mutate()` etc. on a lazy Arrow or DuckDB table, typically code or year lists
(`%in% !!codes`, `>= !!min_date`). To filter on `pnr` against the whole cohort,
use `semi_join(tibble(pnr = cohort_pnrs), by = "pnr", copy = TRUE)` instead: it
takes a local table directly and needs no `!!`. The full explanation is in
[Functions: overview](function-guide.qmd#bang-bang-two-exclamation-marks).
:::

## 9. `nmi_count` is not `nmi` {#nmi-count}

If your dataset has both a Nordic Multimorbidity Index (NMI) score and a count
of conditions, they are not the same variable and are not interchangeable:

  | Variable    | What it is                                                                                                                                                                                                 | Source                  |
  | ----------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------- |
  | `nmi`       | Weighted score that predicts mortality: the Nordic Multimorbidity Index (Kristensen et al., *Clin Epidemiol* 2022). 50 predictors with individual weights; lung cancer counts e.g. 19 points, type 2 diabetes 2. | See [NMI page](nmi.qmd) |
  | `nmi_count` | Unweighted count of the number of conditions a person has been diagnosed with                                                                                                                              | Calculated separately   |

If you use `nmi_count` in your regression model instead of `nmi`, you are
adjusting for something different than you think - and you get no error message.

## 10. Immortal time bias - exposure defined using the future {#immortal-time-bias}

**Immortal time bias** arises when a person is given follow-up time during which
they could not, by construction, have had the outcome. There is no error and no
warning, only an effect estimate that looks too good. It is easy to do with
register data, because you define the groups looking back at what eventually
happened.

An example with made-up numbers. Question: does bariatric surgery lower
mortality in people with type 2 diabetes (T2D)? You take everyone diagnosed with
T2D in 2010, split them into a surgery group (had surgery at some point during
follow-up) and a no-surgery group, and start counting follow-up for everyone at
the diagnosis date.

To land in the surgery group, a person had to survive long enough to be
operated. Say the average wait from diagnosis to surgery is 2 years. Those 2
years are *immortal*: anyone who died in that window never reached surgery and
so fell into the no-surgery group instead. The surgery group has been given
about 2 years of guaranteed-alive person-time, labelled as surgery time.

  | Group                                           | Deaths | Person-years | Rate (per 1000 py) |
  | ----------------------------------------------- | ------ | ------------ | ------------------ |
  | Surgery (immortal time counted as surgery time) | 24     | 12,000       | 2.0                |
  | No surgery (immortal time left out)             | 51     | 13,000       | 3.9                |
  | Surgery (time correctly aligned)                | 24     | 8,000        | 3.0                |
  | No surgery (immortal time moved here)           | 51     | 17,000       | 3.0                |

Correctly aligned, the 4,000 pre-surgery person-years count as no-surgery time,
and the rates are identical (3.0): surgery does nothing. Counting those 4,000
immortal person-years as surgery time drops its rate to 2.0, leaves the
no-surgery rate at 3.9, and makes surgery look 49% protective (rate ratio 0.51).
The "effect" comes from the misaligned time zero, not from surgery.

The fix is to align time zero: eligibility, exposure assignment and start of
follow-up must coincide.

- **Risk-set (incidence-density) matching:** start each person's follow-up at
  the moment they become exposed, and assign each comparator the *same* index
  date (the core rule in [Comparison cohort](comparison-cohort.qmd)).
- **Treat exposure as time-varying:** the person contributes *unexposed*
  person-time until surgery, then *exposed* time after - never exposed time
  before they were exposed (see [Time-varying variables](time-varying.qmd)).

Defining a *baseline covariate* from post-index information is the same error
(e.g. the Open Source Diabetes Classifier, OSDC diabetes type, see [OSDC](osdc.qmd)). Whenever
a variable is built from the future, ask whether you are conditioning on the
person having survived to see it. Background: [Hernán & Robins, *What If*,
§3.6](https://miguelhernan.org/whatifbook) (target trial, time zero).

## 11. `year` is a folder name, not a date {#year-is-not-a-date}

In a register converted to parquet with fastreg, `year` says which yearly file a
row came from. Filtering on it is fast, because only the files for those years
are read, but it does not tell you when anything happened. `year == 2020` in BEF
does not say which quarterly snapshot you have. When the timing matters, use the
register's own date column (`hf_vfra` in the education register, UDDA, `d_inddto` in `lpr_adm`,
`referencetid` in BEF). The two uses look identical in the code.

It is only a year at all if the register arrived as one file per year. Some
registers arrive as a single file covering everything, and then every row
carries the same `year` whatever its date. In the delivery this guide was
written from, `dodsaars` spans 1970 to 2001 and says 2024 on every row, and
`lpr_a_kontakt` is one file holding every contact that ended in 2017 or later,
so counting by `year` puts LPR1 (the oldest format of the National Patient Register), LPR2, MiniPAS (records from private hospitals)
and LPR3 contacts in the same single year.

Check with `count(year)` before you filter on it. One value means the column
labels the delivery, not the data, and a year filter will return everything or
nothing. Use the register's own date column instead, `kont_starttidspunkt` in
`lpr_a_kontakt`. It is per register: `lpr_diag` in the same delivery really is
split by year and filters correctly.

Why four reporting systems end up in one file, and how to filter them, is
explained in [Understand LPR](understand-lpr.qmd#lpr-a-format). How the `year`
column is made is in [Phase 4 - Reading a register that is split by
year](file-formats.qmd#year-column).

## 12. Published totals for the same thing do not agree {#published-totals}

Official publications can give more than one number for what sounds like the
same thing, because the underlying population differs. For 2005,
*Hospital statistics 2005* reports 6,336,000 outpatient visits; the web-based
*Health data* retrieval system reports 1,894,441 outpatient contacts for the
same year, a difference of more than 3-fold. The first includes psychiatric
wards and excludes private hospitals, the second does the opposite ([Lynge et al.
2011](https://doi.org/10.1177/1403494811401482), "The Danish National Patient
Register", *Scand J Public Health* 39(Suppl 7):30-33).

::: {.callout-warning}
**Do not use a published aggregate as ground truth for your own extraction
without checking its exact population.** If your row count from `lpr_a_kontakt`
does not match a number you found in a DST or Sundhedsdatastyrelsen (Danish
Health Data Authority) publication, the mismatch may be the publication's population
definition (which wards, which hospital types, which patient type), not a bug
in your code. Check what the publication actually counted before assuming your
extraction is wrong.
:::

## 13. `lpr_a_kontakt`/`lpr_a_diagnose` are not pure LPR3 {#lpr-a-not-pure-lpr3}

The name suggests these tables hold LPR3 data only. They do not: LPR_A also
carries older LPR1, LPR2 and MiniPAS (private-hospital) rows, reloaded into
the same table and tagged by `lprindberetningssystem`, for contacts that ended
in 2017 or later ([DST's remark on
LPR_A_KONTAKT](https://www.dst.dk/extranet/ForskningVariabellister/Bemaerkning/LPR_A_KONTAKT%20-%20Landspatientregistret%20%28LPR3%29%20-Kontaktoplysninger%20omkring%20de%20enkelte%20kontakter.html)).
See [Understand LPR](understand-lpr.qmd#lpr-a-format) for what that means for
your extract.

If you combine LPR2 (`lpr_adm`) and LPR_A without filtering, the same contacts
get counted twice - once from each table. Filter both `lpr_a_kontakt` and
`lpr_a_diagnose` to `lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3"` before using them
alongside `lpr_adm`/`lpr_diag`:

```r
lpr3_k <- lpr_a_kontakt %>%
  filter(lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3")   # keep only genuine LPR3 rows
lpr3_d <- lpr_a_diagnose %>%
  filter(lprindberetningssystem == "LPR3")   # same column on the diagnosis table
```

::: {.callout-warning}
**The filter can drop real contacts.** Your own `lpr_adm` delivery can end
earlier than DST's LPR2 files do (31 March 2019), in which case the simple
filter above silently drops real, unique contacts along with the duplicates.
See [Extract from
LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd#lpr3-filter-caveat) for how to check your own
delivery's coverage before trusting it. On DARTER (project 708421) specifically, see [DARTER
pitfalls, 3](darter-pitfalls.qmd#lpr3-lprindberetningssystem) for a worked
fix.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Check that `lprindberetningssystem` is in your delivery"}
Deliveries differ between projects, and `lprindberetningssystem` is not always
included: it has been reported missing from `lpr_a_kontakt` in a delivery where
`lpr_a_diagnose` had it. Check both tables before you rely on the filter:

```r
# head(0) %>% collect() fetches the column names with zero rows; colnames() on a
# lazy Arrow table after rename_with() can come back empty
"lprindberetningssystem" %in% names(lpr_a_kontakt %>% head(0) %>% collect())   # TRUE if the column is there
"lprindberetningssystem" %in% names(lpr_a_diagnose %>% head(0) %>% collect())
```

If it is missing, ask DST to add the variable to your delivery.
:::

## 14. LPR2 contacts that never closed are not in `lpr_adm` {#lpr2-open-contacts}

`lpr_adm` and `lpr_diag` hold closed contacts only. A contact that was still
open is in separate tables, `uaf_adm` and `uaf_diag`, and one that never closed
never reaches `lpr_adm`. Sundhedsdatastyrelsen counted just under 192,000 LPR2
contacts still open in September 2020 ([data quality report on the
transition](https://cdn1.gopublic.dk/sundhedsdatastyrelsen/media/16445/Datakvalitetsrapport%20om%20LPR%202019%20_%20overgangen%20fra%20LPR2%20til%20LPR3.pdf),
section 6.1.2). Read only `lpr_adm` and you miss their diagnoses, with no error.
Stacking every year of `uaf_adm` goes wrong the other way and counts a contact
more than once. How the tables are filed is in [Understand
LPR](understand-lpr.qmd#lpr2-open-contacts), and a recipe that reads them
without double counting is in [Extract from
LPR](extract-from-lpr.qmd#step-1-open-contacts).

## If the code stopped with an error {#something-actually-broke}

Most pitfalls above are cases where the code runs and the answer is wrong. If
you have a red error message, or a result that came back empty, go to
[Troubleshooting](troubleshooting.qmd). To check a new delivery against several
of these pitfalls at once, use [Check your delivery](delivery-check.qmd).
